analysis.one_liner: Gave Senate candidates full public campaign funding in exchange for refusing private contributions.
analysis.headline: Introduced April 5, 2001 with 4 cosponsors, the bill never got a hearing, markup, or vote before the 107th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have let Senate candidates who collect a large number of small $5 contributions from voters receive full public funding for their campaigns, in exchange for giving up private donations and personal spending. It also gave those candidates free and discounted broadcast airtime, banned national party committees from raising unregulated "soft money," tightened disclosure of attack ads run by outside groups, and strengthened the Federal Election Commission's enforcement powers. The bill was referred to the Senate Rules and Administration Committee and never received any further action.
analysis.who_benefits: Senate candidates without personal fortunes or access to wealthy donors: anyone who could gather enough small qualifying contributions from residents would receive a public campaign grant (up to roughly $4.4 million for a general election, adjusted for state population and inflation), free prime-time broadcast time, and 50%-discounted ad rates. Voters would gain too: the bill would have banned national party soft money, forced faster disclosure of who paid for issue and independent ads, and required candidates in privately funded ads to state on camera that they declined public funding. The bill's own findings argued this would reduce the disproportionate influence of monied interests over legislation. [S3][S2]
analysis.who_benefits_short: Candidates without wealthy donors, and voters

how_it_helps.text: Senate candidates who qualify by collecting at least 1,000 (or 0.25% of their state's voting-age population in) $5 contributions from state residents would receive full public funding for primary, runoff, and general elections, and would be barred from taking private contributions or using personal wealth beyond a small seed-money allowance.

Clean money candidates would be entitled to free broadcast time (30 minutes in the primary, 60 minutes in the general election, in prime viewing hours) and could buy additional ads at no more than 50% of the lowest candidate rate, paid for by broadcasters.

The bill would prohibit national party committees from soliciting or spending soft money, bar candidates and federal officeholders from soliciting unregulated funds or funneling money through tax-exempt groups, and cap what party committees may spend in elections involving clean money candidates.

Outside groups running issue ads or independent expenditures in Senate races would face rapid 24-to-48-hour disclosure of who funded them, and the definition of an 'independent expenditure' would be tightened so ads could not dodge the rules.

If a privately funded opponent or outside groups outspent a clean money candidate beyond 125% of the public grant, the candidate would automatically receive matching public funds, capped at 200% of the original grant.

The bill would restructure the Federal Election Commission, give it authority to seek court injunctions and issue subpoenas, require audits, and raise penalties for campaign finance violations, including up to 5 years' imprisonment for misusing public campaign funds.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers would fund the campaign grants through a new Senate Election Fund in the Treasury, financed by appropriations 'in such sums as are necessary.' Broadcasters would bear the cost of mandatory free airtime and half-price ad rates. Political parties and large donors would lose soft money and other unregulated channels for influencing Senate elections. [S3]

drawbacks.text: The public financing would be paid for by appropriations with no set limit ('such sums as are necessary'), so taxpayers would be financing political campaign advertising every two years, a cost an honest supporter would have to defend.

A clean money candidate's grant is capped (at the lesser of $4.4 million or a population-based amount), and matching funds top out at 200% of the grant, so a self-funded billionaire opponent could still substantially outspend a publicly funded candidate; the cap also buys far less advertising in expensive media markets than in cheap ones, even with the small-state adjustment.

Requiring broadcasters to donate free airtime and sell ads at half price, and limiting how candidates and parties may spend money, raised substantial First Amendment objections that the bill never got the chance to answer in committee or in court.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade was real: a modest, recurring taxpayer cost and restrictions on how campaigns and parties spend money, in exchange for replacing big-donor financing with small-donor-qualified public grants for every Senate race. The design had genuine weak points, especially the spending cap and the 200% matching-fund ceiling, which could leave a clean money candidate outgunned by a self-funded opponent. But the bill died in committee without a hearing or markup, so none of these costs or design flaws were ever tested in debate, and the structural problem it targeted, the bill's own findings said private contributions gave monied interests unequal access to lawmakers, was left intact. [S3][S5]

outcome.mechanism: It was read twice and referred to the Senate Rules and Administration Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Paul Wellstone introduced the Clean Money, Clean Elections Act on April 5, 2001, joined by Senators Kerry, Clinton, and Cantwell; the bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Rules and Administration the same day.
The complete action history shows no further action: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote at any point before the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incumbent senators and the big donors and interests that fund them were better off, because the private-financing system and party soft money channels this bill would have dismantled stayed in place. Congress did separately enact a partial soft-money ban in 2002 through a different bill, but the public financing at the heart of this bill never advanced again in this form.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Incumbent senators and big campaign donors

for.name: Sen. Paul Wellstone
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Clean Money, Clean Elections Act and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

against.name: Senate Committee on Rules and Administration
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day it was introduced and took no further action for the remainder of the 107th Congress.

against.name: Sen. Christopher Dodd
against.role: Chair, Senate Rules and Administration Committee (from June 2001)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for committee consideration during his chairmanship.

sides.party_line_note: All five of the bill's sponsors and cosponsors were Senate Democrats, no Republican signed on, and no vote ever occurred to test broader support; a separate soft-money bill did pass with bipartisan support later in the same Congress, but this bill's public-financing core drew no Republican backing.

industries.note: The bill would have required stations to donate substantial free prime time to clean money candidates and sell them additional ads at up to 50% off the lowest candidate rate, with limits on preemption. Broadcasters would have absorbed that cost directly, which is why their interest ran against a provision whose benefit was more candidate speech reaching voters.

National parties would have been barred from raising or spending soft money, parties could not route funds to tax-exempt groups, and party spending in Senate races with clean money candidates would be capped at 10% of the public grant. Parties lost a major funding channel; the bill treated that channel as part of the money-in-politics problem.

industries.industry: Large campaign donors and lobbying interests
industries.note: The bill's stated aim was to eliminate the access that large contributions buy: candidates who opted in could accept no private money beyond small seed contributions, soft money solicitations by federal candidates were banned, and outside spending had to be disclosed within 24 to 48 hours. The bill's own findings said private contributions gave monied interests disproportionate influence over legislation.

Incumbents would have been freed from constant fundraising and fromMass franking-mail restrictions during election years, but they would also lose the donor advantage over challengers that the bill said made Senate elections uncompetitive, and they would have to declare on camera in ads that they declined public funding if they kept taking private money.
